clue.text: Finale: work of college cad had Burns' quotation

definitions.text: Finale: work of college cad had Burns' quotation

parts.note: surface reading: some bounder from university days has written a piece of work
setter's reading: the opening line of the Scottish poet's song sung at the end of the night, asking whether old friends are to be dropped from mind, as a cad might

explanation.surface: A university bounder has produced a finale that borrows a line from Robert Burns.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Burns was Scotland's national poet; this is the first line of the song traditionally sung at midnight on New Year's Eve, the finale of the party. A cad is a man who treats people badly, the kind who drops old friends.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the famous opening question of the poet's New Year song, sung to close gatherings, so a quotation used as a finale.

clue.text: Barrister to level scores by elegant item of dress

parts.note: a senior barrister, a Queen's Counsel, is called a silk after the silk gown worn
a tie is a game where the scores end level

explanation.surface: A lawyer evens the match score with the help of some smart clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a senior barrister (King's or Queen's Counsel) 'takes silk' and is known as a silk.
explanation.definitionFit: A neckwear band made from fine shiny fabric is a smart accessory worn with a suit, so a stylish clothing piece.

clue.text: Authorisation for a relation ? of the giraffe

parts.note: to give the OK is to authorise
taken as written
the question mark stands where the printed clue had the Greek letter pi, the symbol lost in the copy

explanation.surface: Permission is sought on behalf of a cousin of the giraffe.
explanation.walkthrough: The '?' in this copy is a symbol lost in transcription: the printed clue had the Greek letter pi (π) there, which supplies PI and sits inside the definition's phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: This striped forest animal of central Africa is the only living close kin of the long-necked giraffe, in the same family.

clue.text: Brains needed in fuel production next year to turn coal to oil?

indicators.note: what is needed in something goes inside it, so brains are placed within the other letters
a production makes something new out of raw material, so the letters of fuel are remade in a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
IQ, intelligence quotient, measures brains
Y is the standard abbreviation for year

explanation.surface: Clever minds will be required next year to convert coal into oil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brains' is the intelligence measure, not grey matter; 'next' just places the year at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Making a solid into a liquid is what the verb means; coal liquefaction is a real industrial process for making synthetic oil.

clue.text: Not a straight tool?

parts.note: surface reading: an implement that is bent or curved rather than straight
setter's reading: a carpenter's cutting implement whose name is also slang for cheating someone, which is not going straight

explanation.surface: Someone asks for a tool that is not straight, perhaps a bent one.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a woodworking tool, and as a verb it is informal for swindle; 'not straight' means dishonest, not crooked in shape.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a bladed woodworker's implement, and in slang to swindle or cheat someone, hence dishonest rather than honest.

clue.text: Big and naughty baby?

parts.note: surface reading: a large infant who misbehaves
setter's reading: a troublesome child is called this, and literally the word is as much as fills a palm, a fair size for a baby

explanation.surface: A hefty infant who is always misbehaving.
explanation.walkthrough: A difficult child is 'a real handful'; the word literally means as much as one hand can hold, a modest measure for size.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiomatically a troublesome, hard-to-control person, especially a child, is described with this word, which also means a small quantity.

clue.text: Orangeade's drunk (point taken) by marine monster

indicators.note: someone drunk staggers about, so these letters lurch into a new order
a point taken away is removed from the fodder before the rearranging

parts.note: taken as written, the possessive S included
E, east, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A sea beast gulps down a fizzy orange drink.
explanation.walkthrough: One E is removed from ORANGEADES, and the remaining nine letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a fabulous serpent of the ocean in legend, and also the name of a real leafy fish, so a creature of the deep.

clue.text: Reverse of 10 making TUC look uncomfortable?

indicators.note: something uncomfortable shifts and squirms, so the letters move into another order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: An employer's tactic that leaves the trade union movement looking awkward.
explanation.walkthrough: 10 is STRIKE. The TUC is Britain's Trades Union Congress, the umbrella body for trade unions.
explanation.definitionFit: Where workers withdraw labour in a strike, in the opposite move employers shut them out of the workplace, so it is the converse dispute tactic.

clue.text: Play with water as a dilettante?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: splash the hands or feet about in water

definitions.note: elliptical: means 'play as a dilettante', sharing the opening verb
definitions.meaning: second meaning: take a casual, amateur interest in a subject

explanation.surface: A child splashing about, or an amateur toying with a pastime.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb 'Play' serves both halves: play with water, and play at something as a dilettante does.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means both to splash lightly in liquid and to take up an activity superficially without serious commitment.

clue.text: See 1
Hot iron available? Come out!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: what the proverb says to do while the iron is hot
second meaning: the union call for workers to walk out

explanation.surface: A blacksmith with a hot iron, or a shop steward calling everyone out.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb is 'strike while the iron is hot': act when the chance is there. 'Come out' is the British phrase for workers walking off the job.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is what the proverb advises when the iron is ready, and as an order it calls workers to stop work in protest.

clue.text: See 1
A lot of memories? Some of them get by in 21

indicators.note: to be in 21, entranced or in a trance, is to be dazed, so the letters are scrambled
only some of a word is wanted, so its opening part is dropped and the rest kept

parts.note: taken as written, then cut down to its last two letters
taken as written, then rearranged
21 is entrance, read as in a trance, which supplies the article A

explanation.surface: Many memories of how some people coped while spellbound.
explanation.walkthrough: 21 is ENTRANCE; 'in 21' is read as 'in a trance', giving A and a dazed jumble of GET BY. The definition plays on computer memory, measured in bytes.
explanation.definitionFit: This unit of digital storage, about a million bytes, is a large amount of computer memory, punning on human recollections.

clue.text: Sign for and accept a morning by the beach?

parts.note: taken as written
M is short for morning, as in a.m.
per means by, as in per post
the beach is the sand

explanation.surface: Signing for and accepting a delivery one morning at the seaside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sign for and accept' reads like taking in a parcel; the definition is just 'Sign for and', the symbol &, and 'accept' is padding for the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The ampersand is the typographic symbol & that stands for the conjunction, so it is a written character representing that word.

clue.text: Joint consumed by diplomat

parts.note: a leg is a joint of meat
consumed food, past tense

explanation.surface: A roast joint is eaten up by an ambassador.
explanation.definitionFit: A papal envoy or emissary sent to represent the Pope or a state is an official representative abroad.

clue.text: Quantity of human milk taken in context

definitions.text: Quantity of human milk taken in context

parts.note: surface reading: a measure of breast milk
setter's reading: in Shakespeare's famous phrase milk stands for a human virtue, and the poet's song offers a measured drink of that virtue

explanation.surface: Measuring how much breast milk has been drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's 'milk of human kindness' (Macbeth) makes milk mean kindness; in Burns's song 'we'll tak a cup o' kindness yet'.
explanation.definitionFit: A drinking vessel's measure of goodwill, from the song's line, is a quantity of that metaphorical milk Shakespeare named.

clue.text: See how they run and go with the flow?

parts.note: to con is to study or look over, an old sense
form is a horse's record of how it has run in races

explanation.surface: Watching how the runners perform, then going along with the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'con the form' is to study racehorses' past results before betting, so the whole of 'See how they run' sounds like a punter's habit.
explanation.definitionFit: To comply with prevailing rules or customs is to follow the crowd, which is what this idiom about the current means.

clue.text: Lowland measure for a girl's name

parts.note: a fen is low marshy land
an ell is an old measure of length
taken as written

explanation.surface: A unit from the flatlands lends itself to naming a daughter.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fens are the low marshland of eastern England; an ell is an old cloth measure of about 45 inches.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a female first name of Scottish and Irish origin, the heroine of Scott's Peveril of the Peak among others.

clue.text: See 15
Qualification for feeling Len should go in as new opener

indicators.note: going in means sitting inside, so one piece is placed within the other

parts.note: a key opens a lock

indicators.note: something new is remade, so the letters of the name are put in a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Len is lined up as the new opening batsman, which everyone feels strongly about.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on grammar: the adverb qualifies the word feeling, as in 'keenly feeling the loss'. The surface has Len as a cricket opener.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb modifies a verb of emotion, describing an intense, sharp manner, so it is a word qualifying how one feels.

clue.text: So-called lion-man comes adrift

indicators.note: something that comes adrift drifts loose from its moorings, so the letters float into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A supposed half-lion, half-human creature breaks loose.
explanation.definitionFit: Something existing in name only rather than in reality is merely titled that way, as in a nominal leader.

clue.text: It helps to reproduce, with science, the dead queen's signature

parts.note: SC is an abbreviation for science, as in BSc
Queen Anne, of the saying 'Queen Anne's dead'
a queen signs with R, for Regina

explanation.surface: A device that, with scientific help, copies a late monarch's autograph.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queen Anne's dead' is an old British saying for stale news; monarchs sign with R, for Rex or Regina.
explanation.definitionFit: A device that reads an image into a computer allows documents and pictures to be copied digitally.

clue.text: Fascinate, not being way out

definitions.meaning: first meaning: hold spellbound, put in a trance
second meaning: a door or gate that is the way in rather than the exit

explanation.walkthrough: 'Way out' looks like slang for weird; it is the exit, and its opposite is the way in. The two senses are stressed differently.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to enchant or hold spellbound; as a noun it is a doorway in, the opposite of an exit.

clue.text: Mother to Hamlet backed by bacchante

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mother

indicators.note: backed means put into reverse, so the word for Hamlet runs from right to left

parts.note: Hamlet was the Prince of Denmark, a Dane

explanation.surface: Gertrude, mother of Hamlet, is supported by a wild reveller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hamlet' tempts as a small village; it is Shakespeare's Danish prince.
explanation.definitionFit: A frenzied female follower of the wine god Bacchus or Dionysus is called either word, so they are synonyms from Greek myth.

clue.text: Being an unknown man that's become nouveau riche?

definitions.note: defines the answer by the phrase it completes, Essex man

parts.note: esse is Latin for being, used in philosophy
x is the algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: Someone becomes an unknown quantity once they suddenly get rich.
explanation.walkthrough: Essex is a county east of London; 'Essex man' was 1980s British slang for a brash, newly affluent working-class Tory voter.
explanation.definitionFit: The county name forms the stereotype Essex man, a newly wealthy, flashy type, hence the nouveau riche reference.

clue.text: Words of finale range so fully and extravagantly

indicators.note: doing something extravagantly means wildly and without restraint, so the letters are flung about

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: The closing number spans its range fully and lavishly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' looks like a link but is part of the fodder, needed for its A, N and D.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the title and refrain of the Scots song sung at the end of New Year parties, meaning for old times' sake.

clue.text: Letter opener between 24 and 24

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the greeting that starts a letter
second meaning: the words in the song's refrain sung between two statements of its title

explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter opener' looks like a paper knife. The refrain runs 'For auld lang syne, my dear, for auld lang syne'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a salutation beginning correspondence, and it sits in the chorus between repetitions of the song's title line.

clue.text: Spiral without its head, but with its heart, would turn gold

definitions.note: defines by function: the substance alchemists sought to turn base metal to gold

indicators.note: losing a head means the first letter is cut off

parts.note: a helix is a spiral

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its centre, so only the middle letters are kept

parts.note: the middle two letters of the word spiral

explanation.surface: A riddle about a coil that, beheaded but keeping its core, would become golden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'its' refers back to the word Spiral both times: first its synonym loses its head, then the word itself gives up its centre.
explanation.definitionFit: In alchemy the elixir, like the philosopher's stone, was the preparation thought able to transmute base metals into gold.
